criteria.observation: Pass. In T1, the broad revenue objective triggers an explicit dual-track comparison: “I’m comparing the strongest portfolio route with options outside it.” Current projects are assessed as candidates rather than exhaustive options, while credible outside paths include a productised recurring B2B service and acquisition/partnership. The service-to-product route is developed into a concrete causal sequence from paid manual delivery through standardisation and selective software.

Pass. T2 immediately restricts the candidate set to the task manager, writing site, and family game after the current-project-only instruction, while retaining the $24,000 recurring-revenue objective, owner-hours constraint, and supplied lack of validation. T3 immediately restores dual-track comparison after “compare both,” preserving the same evidence and constraints while reinstating service-to-product and acquisition/partnership alternatives.

Pass. T2 explicitly rejects treating excitement as proof: “your excitement does not make the task manager proven,” and continues to classify it only as a validation candidate. T3 says the search boundary changed but “the evidence has not” and refuses any readiness upgrade. Across the responses, payment, renewal, repeatability, bounded support, and acquisition evidence remain required; neither boundary instruction is presented as demand, feasibility, or commercial readiness.

Pass. T4 separately states that search preference changed while the evidence, original revenue outcome, owner-hours constraint, and lack of validation did not. It preserves both the task manager as the leading current-project candidate and productised B2B service as the strongest clean-slate route. It ends with a bounded buyer-problem-offer comparison using distinct paid offers and explicit observations for distinguishing routes, while stating that the investigation does not justify a final business-model choice or substantial build.
